splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps agency deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions in criminal sentencing guidelines.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's anti-defendant interpretations of ambiguous Guidelines provisions or instead apply the rule of lenity in favor of the defendant. This matters because it determines whether agencies can effectively expand criminal liability through interpretive guidance rather than through formal lawmaking.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability through interpretive guidance.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary takes precedence over the rule of lenity, allowing the Commission's anti-defendant interpretations to control even in ambiguous cases.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy, based on Application Note 1's expansion of the guideline text.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which adds conspiracy and attempt to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid authoritative interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor, or whether it impermissibly expands the unambiguous guideline text. This affects thousands of career-offender designations under federal sentencing guidelines.

positions.label: Commentary is authoritative and includes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and that 'controlled substance offense' includes conspiracy, attempt, and aiding and abetting, warranting deference under Stinson.

positions.label: Guideline text is unambiguous and excludes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that the text of § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and that Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline beyond its plain meaning, so conspiracy convictions cannot serve as career-offender predicates.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: A deep circuit split exists on whether a defendant must meet all three criminal-history disqualifiers in § 3553(f)(1) to be ineligible for safety-valve relief, or whether meeting any single criterion is disqualifying. This directly affects whether defendants facing mandatory minimum sentences can receive lower sentences and creates geographic disparities in criminal sentencing.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' means 'and,' so a defendant is disqualified from safety-valve relief only if all three criminal-history criteria are satisfied.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive or distributive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as distributive or disjunctive in context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state statute covers substances not listed in the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires that the underlying substance be federally controlled, or whether any state-law drug offense qualifies regardless of whether the substance appears on federal schedules. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for thousands of defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: State offenses qualify regardless of federal scheduling
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines broadly define 'controlled substance offense' to include any state drug offense, without requiring the substance to be controlled under federal law, because there is no textual basis to graft a federal-law limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: Substance must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance involved is also controlled under federal law, requiring a match between state and federal drug schedules.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held it belongs to the estate, creating a split with circuits that protect debtors' post-petition appreciation upon good-faith conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that under the broad scope of § 541(a) and the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A), post-petition appreciation in property value inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A) protects good-faith converting debtors by limiting the estate to the value of property as of the original petition date, so post-petition appreciation belongs to the debtor.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the First Step Act's non-retroactive anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's policy statement in U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) validly authorizes such relief.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's elimination of mandatory stacked 25-year sentences for multiple § 924(c) counts, can support a compassionate release motion. The Seventh Circuit holds the Commission exceeded its statutory authority in promulgating § 1B1.13(b)(6), while other circuits have permitted such changes to contribute to compassionate release findings.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law cannot constitute an extraordinary and compelling reason for sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A), and that the Sentencing Commission exceeded its authority in attempting to authorize such relief.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes can contribute to compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered, alone or in combination with other factors, as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appellate deadline applies to an appeal from the denial of a motion for attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment in a criminal case.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Hyde Amendment, which permits criminal defendants to recover fees for frivolous or bad-faith prosecutions, triggers the civil 30-day appeal deadline or the criminal 14-day deadline. The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view applying the civil deadline because the fee motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment fee motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that because the Hyde Amendment motion arises from a criminal case, the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) governs.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a federal prisoner challenging a Bureau of Prisons decision regarding conditions of confinement (such as denial of transfer to prerelease custody under the First Step Act) must proceed via habeas corpus or may use civil rights remedies.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy when a federal prisoner challenges BOP decisions that affect the terms or conditions of confinement but do not directly challenge the fact or duration of imprisonment. This affects the procedural vehicle available to thousands of federal prisoners seeking to enforce First Step Act earned-time-credit provisions.

positions.label: Habeas is not the exclusive remedy for conditions challenges
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions of confinement, as opposed to the fact or duration of imprisonment, may proceed through civil rights actions (e.g., Bivens) and are not limited to habeas corpus.

positions.label: Habeas is the proper vehicle for BOP custody decisions
positions.summary: Holds that prisoner challenges to BOP decisions affecting the timing and conditions of release, including First Step Act earned-time-credit determinations, must be brought as habeas claims under 28 U.S.C. § 2241.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose revocation sentences to punish defendants for violations of supervised release, or whether revocation sentences must be justified solely by the need to sanction the breach of trust.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit permits district courts to expressly punish defendants for the conduct underlying supervised release violations, while other circuits hold that revocation sentences should reflect only the breach of the court's trust, not serve as punishment for the new misconduct. This affects the sentencing rationale for hundreds of supervised release revocations annually.

positions.label: Express punishment for violations is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants at revocation for the conduct underlying the supervised release violation, placing the Sixth Circuit at the extreme of the circuit split.

positions.label: Revocation sentences should address breach of trust, not punish
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release revocation sanctions should reflect the defendant's breach of the court's trust rather than serve as punishment for the underlying violation conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability to be locked in by the end of the plan year, or whether actuaries may select or adjust assumptions after that date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by the measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be determined by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), preventing actuaries from retroactively selecting assumptions that increase employer liability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after the measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that actuaries may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, as the statute does not require all assumptions to be locked in by year-end.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: New York Times Co. v. Newspaper & Mail Deliverers'-Publishers' Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the supervision period beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects how federal courts calculate sentencing guidelines at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond each year.

positions.label: Supervised release is tolled during absconding
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, so the clock stops running and the court retains jurisdiction to revoke supervised release after the original term would have expired.

positions.label: Supervised release is not tolled during absconding
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory authority for tolling supervised release when a supervisee absconds, so the term continues to run and expires as originally set regardless of the supervisee's compliance.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: A longstanding 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) — which prohibits raising any claim previously presented in a prior habeas application — when bringing successive § 2255 motions. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than § 2255(h) alone would impose.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the § 2244(b)(1) bar on relitigating previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, categorically barring any claim that was presented in a prior motion.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, so they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits have disagreed on when and whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The resolution affects the ability of candidates to challenge election administration rules before an election occurs, with implications for mail-in voting rules, ballot counting deadlines, and other election procedures nationwide.

positions.label: Candidates have standing for pre-election challenges
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge election rules before Election Day because the allegedly unlawful counting of ballots directly harms their competitive interests.

positions.label: Candidates lack standing absent concrete vote-dilution injury
positions.summary: Holds that candidates must demonstrate a concrete, particularized injury from the challenged election rule and cannot rely solely on generalized competitive interest to establish standing.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that orders denying motions to seal medical records are immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of 'high order' that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment, since the information would already have been publicly disclosed. Other circuits have taken varying approaches to immediate appealability of sealing orders.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable because medical privacy is a value of high order that cannot be adequately vindicated after final judgment, as the privacy interest would be irretrievably lost once records are publicly disclosed.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's requirements because the party can seek review after final judgment or through mandamus, and the interest does not rise to the level required for interlocutory appeal.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: Circuits have applied different standards for evaluating discrimination claims in business and hospitality contexts. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve the Second Circuit's approach, suggesting a circuit split on liability standards, available remedies, and the scope of protections for customers in service industries.

positions.label: Broader liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a broader standard for discrimination claims in hospitality or business establishments, potentially allowing claims based on a wider range of conduct.

positions.label: Narrower liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a narrower standard requiring a more specific showing of discriminatory conduct before liability attaches in hospitality or business settings.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether state laws categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violate the Equal Protection Clause, and what level of scrutiny applies to such classifications.
splits.description: Circuits are beginning to divide on the constitutionality of state laws that categorically prohibit transgender athletes from competing on teams consistent with their gender identity. This split implicates the level of scrutiny applicable to sex-based and transgender classifications and whether as-applied challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.

positions.label: Laws likely violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that categorical bans on transgender women in women's sports likely violate the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender individuals who have medically mitigated their sex-based biological advantages.

positions.label: Laws are constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that such laws are a permissible exercise of state authority to maintain fair competition in women's sports based on biological sex differences.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
